final_answer:
In a free market, the price of a good or service is determined by the interaction of supply and demand. When the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, the market reaches equilibrium, establishing the equilibrium price. If the price is above equilibrium, a surplus occurs because suppliers want to sell more than consumers are willing to buy. If the price is below equilibrium, a shortage occurs because consumers want to buy more than suppliers are willing to sell.

When a government imposes a price ceiling, it sets a maximum price that can be charged for a good or service. If this ceiling is set below the equilibrium price, it creates a shortage because suppliers are unwilling or unable to supply as much as consumers want to buy. This can lead to long lines, black markets, or reduced product quality. If the price ceiling is set above the equilibrium price, it has little to no effect because the market would naturally adjust to the equilibrium price. Governments may impose price ceilings to make essential goods more affordable, but it can lead to unintended consequences such as those mentioned.
